I think the most salient things to try are running it with/without `--device_allocator=debug`, with/without `--device_allocator=caching`, and with/without `--device_allocator=caching --device_allocator=debug`. If we can fill out that matrix it'll help narrow down what's happening and then if it's not something obvious we can dogfood the new trace replay stuff to ensure we can more easily triage things like this in the future.

My first thought was that we were generating code assuming that buffers were zeroed as without the caching allocator they almost always are and it'd be hard to spot. I added the `debug` allocator which scribbles all memory that's allocated and that should be able to rule out such issues irrespective of the caching allocator as no buffer our generated code sees will ever start zeroed.

My next thought was that there was some state leak somewhere causing buffers to remain in use by two places that both thought they had unique buffers but after an audit I couldn't find out how that's possible in the runtime side (though it may be possible in the python side!). The trace replay tool should be able to reproduce that kind of issue (you can make multiple calls with the same buffers and chain buffers between calls, simulating the reuse the python layer is doing) but I couldn't get it to happen. TSAN may help here if we can get a reproducer or run the original stuff with it enabled (doubtful in python land).

My next thought was that this was unique to the set_params behavior in this example - the model includes constants but then they get overridden with the external values. Looking at the program we generate, though, this seems unlikely as it's embarrassingly bad (whoops) and copies in the set_params args every invocation such that there shouldn't be any way for future changes to the params to impact model execution.

Finally, I got suspicious that this may be target dependent. I'm on an AMD CPU and don't enable host features so it's possible this relates to a codegen bug that only triggers on certain archs. For example if some crazy masking/padding/etc path kicks in on certain vector widths and doesn't properly restrict its range if it started seeing non-zero values it may produce the wrong results. Alright, I believe I've found the root cause.  A few things to note:

1) The values themselves are not actually changing.  For example, in the list of hashed contents I posted [above](https://github.com/openxla/iree/issues/12161#issuecomment-1464502638), where the contents seem to change to incorrect values, it's actually the case that we are pointing to the wrong buffers altogether.

2) This incorrect pointer is grabbed inside [`iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_find_and_take_buffer`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L169).  If all of the params were of different size, or we scanned in the same order, we would potentially "accidentally" grab the correct values.  Because we scan in reverse order and we see a buffer of the same size as another parameter, we end up grabbing the wrong buffer and returning it.

3) Wouldn't this mean rather than values changing, we'd likely see at least one swap places?  Yup!  If you look back to the list of hashed contents I posted [above](https://github.com/openxla/iree/issues/12161#issuecomment-1464502638), you'll see some of the values (e.g. `738060328589878804`) don't just disappear in the bad runs -- they change places.  Too many numbers or we might have noticed earlier!

The language around "free" and the logic we're applying to determine whether to return the buffer seems incorrect at [this stage](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L165) (e.g. doing fairly coarse checks such as whether the buffer is the right size).  It doesn't seem like these buffers should be "free" at all (we're still using them, after all); also, it seems semantically like we are wanting to find an existing buffer, not a free one.

That being said, I don't know enough about how this is intended to work to know whether this is actually wrong at a higher level (and if it is, what the correct calls would be).  If someone (presumably @benvanik) can validate whether my intuition here is correct and what we probably _should_ be doing instead, I can look into it more and try to get a fix.  Also happy to report back any tracebacks or logic flows that got me to a particular place if that's easier than reproducing on your own.

RE iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_find_and_take_buffer, I'm not sure I follow - can you clarify what you mean by "incorrect pointer" and "wrong buffer" - the only things that classify a "correct buffer" are its type, usage, and size, and any buffer matching those 3 things is correct.

RE "free" I'm also not sure I follow - the list only tracks buffers that are free for use (or should), so it's a free list - any buffer in that list should definitely not be in use. iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_take_buffer_at (called by iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_find_and_take_buffer) removes the buffer it takes from the list because it's in use, and the only thing that (should) add it back to the list is iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_push_buffer that gets called when the buffer is released back to the pool when it is no longer in use.

I'm still not sure I see the bug (but don't doubt there is one).

Phew.  I've investigated seemingly every relevant twist and turn here and tried to boil it down to the essential.  I think I understand the intent of the allocator and how this flow should work now.  It wasn't clear to me whether the allocator was intended to re-use these same Python buffers and their respective values across calls, or whether it was to do something simpler.  I'm pretty sure the former isn't true, and it probably made my message above confusing.

# The First Call to `set_params`

Everything starts with the call to `set_params` in Python.  Since this is a function defined in the model, we go through [`FunctionInvoker.__call__`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/e87f194f3e36ae20cbf94ea075765221e67b3850/runtime/bindings/python/iree/runtime/function.py#L113).  After setting up the invocation context, we [pack the arguments](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/e87f194f3e36ae20cbf94ea075765221e67b3850/runtime/bindings/python/iree/runtime/function.py#L115).  This is where the data structures that ultimately cause trouble are initialized.

Across the boundary from Python into C++, we enter [`Pack`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/e87f194f3e36ae20cbf94ea075765221e67b3850/runtime/bindings/python/invoke.cc#L593).  Inside `Pack`, we loop through the individual positional arguments and [call into the packing function](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/e87f194f3e36ae20cbf94ea075765221e67b3850/runtime/bindings/python/invoke.cc#L613) on that argument.  This packing function resolves down to [`GetGenericPackCallbackForNdarray`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/e87f194f3e36ae20cbf94ea075765221e67b3850/runtime/bindings/python/invoke.cc#L381).  Here, we [call out](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/e87f194f3e36ae20cbf94ea075765221e67b3850/runtime/bindings/python/invoke.cc#L401) to `AllocateBufferCopy`.  This goes through [vtable dispatch via `iree_hal_allocator_allocate_buffer`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/97779d7f494660f88864b035475ec77a1e54c6c8/runtime/src/iree/hal/allocator.c#L217) to bring us to the caching allocator's [`iree_hal_caching_allocator_allocate_buffer`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L688) function.

Next, we [call to `iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_acquire`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L752-L754), which [calls into `iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_find_and_take_buffer`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L248-L253) (definition [here](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L169)).  For each of our 8 arguments in this first call, we fall through with a NULL value.  This causes `existing_buffer` to evaluate as false, and we avoid taking [the branch that would exit the function](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L260-L265). Next, since no existing buffer was found, [we copy `initial_data` into the buffer](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L283-L285).  This all works as expected.

Once `set_params` exits, the ref count for our argument list drops to 0 and the list is released.  This ultimately causes [`iree_vm_list_destroy`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/af60bfbfeeffbc56fbf6cc41b6af12e0842edc4b/runtime/src/iree/vm/list.c#L236) to be called, which ultimately calls [`iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_release`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L305) on the items in the list.

# The Second Call to `set_params`

Everything proceeds the same as in the first call until we get to [`iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_find_and_take_buffer`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L169).  Unlike the first example, we now no longer fall through for each argument.  Instead, the caching allocator finds an appropriate buffer that was released earlier and returns it.  Upstream, this causes the [check for `existing_buffer`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L260-L265) to evaluate as `true` now, and we return.

There's a problem though: because we exited the function early, we never [copied in `initial_data`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L282-L286); this means we're just re-using data from earlier.  Since some of our parameters' buffers look the same from the caching allocator's point of view, and we're iterating in reverse order, the allocator ends up choosing a buffer that was previously assigned to a different parameter (what I called the "wrong" buffer earlier), causing parameter values to be swapped.

Based on the intention of the allocator, I now see that the buffer choice isn't wrong per se; it's just that we need to then fill the buffer with `initial_data`, if passed.

Does this look right to you @benvanik?

Thank you, Daniel - I think you've identified the bug. Thank you for taking the time to understand how all of this works through the Python layer.

Indeed, I'm not seeing where anything would be handling the initial data in the found case. This likely doesn't happen much (or at all) in the steady state of operation but just at these edges (https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L260).

you are absolutely correct and that's the ticket! I'll get this fixed now!

Alright, I believe I've found the root cause.  A few things to note:

1) The values themselves are not actually changing.  For example, in the list of hashed contents I posted [above](https://github.com/openxla/iree/issues/12161#issuecomment-1464502638), where the contents seem to change to incorrect values, it's actually the case that we are pointing to the wrong buffers altogether.

2) This incorrect pointer is grabbed inside [`iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_find_and_take_buffer`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L169).  If all of the params were of different size, or we scanned in the same order, we would potentially "accidentally" grab the correct values.  Because we scan in reverse order and we see a buffer of the same size as another parameter, we end up grabbing the wrong buffer and returning it.

3) Wouldn't this mean rather than values changing, we'd likely see at least one swap places?  Yup!  If you look back to the list of hashed contents I posted [above](https://github.com/openxla/iree/issues/12161#issuecomment-1464502638), you'll see some of the values (e.g. `738060328589878804`) don't just disappear in the bad runs -- they change places.  Too many numbers or we might have noticed earlier!

The language around "free" and the logic we're applying to determine whether to return the buffer seems incorrect at [this stage](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L165) (e.g. doing fairly coarse checks such as whether the buffer is the right size).  It doesn't seem like these buffers should be "free" at all (we're still using them, after all); also, it seems semantically like we are wanting to find an existing buffer, not a free one.

That being said, I don't know enough about how this is intended to work to know whether this is actually wrong at a higher level (and if it is, what the correct calls would be).  If someone (presumably @benvanik) can validate whether my intuition here is correct and what we probably _should_ be doing instead, I can look into it more and try to get a fix.  Also happy to report back any tracebacks or logic flows that got me to a particular place if that's easier than reproducing on your own.

This is really useful information @dellis23 - thanks for digging in - I don't think any of us noticed the data changes you point out!

RE iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_find_and_take_buffer, I'm not sure I follow - can you clarify what you mean by "incorrect pointer" and "wrong buffer" - the only things that classify a "correct buffer" are its type, usage, and size, and any buffer matching those 3 things is correct.

RE "free" I'm also not sure I follow - the list only tracks buffers that are free for use (or should), so it's a free list - any buffer in that list should definitely not be in use. iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_take_buffer_at (called by iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_find_and_take_buffer) removes the buffer it takes from the list because it's in use, and the only thing that (should) add it back to the list is iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_push_buffer that gets called when the buffer is released back to the pool when it is no longer in use.

I'm still not sure I see the bug (but don't doubt there is one).

One thing to try now that you're debugging at this level would be to print out the buffers as they are acquired/released to the free list - if you see two acquires without a release or something that'd indicate what you're talking about above (I think?) and would be incorrect, but if they're all perfectly paired (acquire A acquire B release A release B etc) then that's likely not the issue.

Phew.  I've investigated seemingly every relevant twist and turn here and tried to boil it down to the essential.  I think I understand the intent of the allocator and how this flow should work now.  It wasn't clear to me whether the allocator was intended to re-use these same Python buffers and their respective values across calls, or whether it was to do something simpler.  I'm pretty sure the former isn't true, and it probably made my message above confusing.

# The First Call to `set_params`

Everything starts with the call to `set_params` in Python.  Since this is a function defined in the model, we go through [`FunctionInvoker.__call__`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/e87f194f3e36ae20cbf94ea075765221e67b3850/runtime/bindings/python/iree/runtime/function.py#L113).  After setting up the invocation context, we [pack the arguments](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/e87f194f3e36ae20cbf94ea075765221e67b3850/runtime/bindings/python/iree/runtime/function.py#L115).  This is where the data structures that ultimately cause trouble are initialized.

Across the boundary from Python into C++, we enter [`Pack`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/e87f194f3e36ae20cbf94ea075765221e67b3850/runtime/bindings/python/invoke.cc#L593).  Inside `Pack`, we loop through the individual positional arguments and [call into the packing function](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/e87f194f3e36ae20cbf94ea075765221e67b3850/runtime/bindings/python/invoke.cc#L613) on that argument.  This packing function resolves down to [`GetGenericPackCallbackForNdarray`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/e87f194f3e36ae20cbf94ea075765221e67b3850/runtime/bindings/python/invoke.cc#L381).  Here, we [call out](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/e87f194f3e36ae20cbf94ea075765221e67b3850/runtime/bindings/python/invoke.cc#L401) to `AllocateBufferCopy`.  This goes through [vtable dispatch via `iree_hal_allocator_allocate_buffer`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/97779d7f494660f88864b035475ec77a1e54c6c8/runtime/src/iree/hal/allocator.c#L217) to bring us to the caching allocator's [`iree_hal_caching_allocator_allocate_buffer`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L688) function.

Next, we [call to `iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_acquire`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L752-L754), which [calls into `iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_find_and_take_buffer`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L248-L253) (definition [here](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L169)).  For each of our 8 arguments in this first call, we fall through with a NULL value.  This causes `existing_buffer` to evaluate as false, and we avoid taking [the branch that would exit the function](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L260-L265). Next, since no existing buffer was found, [we copy `initial_data` into the buffer](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L283-L285).  This all works as expected.

Once `set_params` exits, the ref count for our argument list drops to 0 and the list is released.  This ultimately causes [`iree_vm_list_destroy`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/af60bfbfeeffbc56fbf6cc41b6af12e0842edc4b/runtime/src/iree/vm/list.c#L236) to be called, which ultimately calls [`iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_release`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L305) on the items in the list.

# The Second Call to `set_params`

Everything proceeds the same as in the first call until we get to [`iree_hal_caching_allocator_pool_find_and_take_buffer`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L169).  Unlike the first example, we now no longer fall through for each argument.  Instead, the caching allocator finds an appropriate buffer that was released earlier and returns it.  Upstream, this causes the [check for `existing_buffer`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L260-L265) to evaluate as `true` now, and we return.

There's a problem though: because we exited the function early, we never [copied in `initial_data`](https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L282-L286); this means we're just re-using data from earlier.  Since some of our parameters' buffers look the same from the caching allocator's point of view, and we're iterating in reverse order, the allocator ends up choosing a buffer that was previously assigned to a different parameter (what I called the "wrong" buffer earlier), causing parameter values to be swapped.

Based on the intention of the allocator, I now see that the buffer choice isn't wrong per se; it's just that we need to then fill the buffer with `initial_data`, if passed.

Does this look right to you @benvanik?

Thank you, Daniel - I think you've identified the bug. Thank you for taking the time to understand how all of this works through the Python layer.

Indeed, I'm not seeing where anything would be handling the initial data in the found case. This likely doesn't happen much (or at all) in the steady state of operation but just at these edges (https://github.com/openxla/iree/blob/689e0fa332fda93404462636fa60fdaf96486aa8/runtime/src/iree/hal/utils/caching_allocator.c#L260).
